utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness 2, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Dieckmann, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to inform the Chamber that, with the excellent guidance of the Registry, we have been able to produce a list of documents the Defence of Bajrush Morina intends to or may use during cross-examination; and for easy identification of the material, we would like to give every one of the parties one of the copies, and I would refer to the ID on the this paper when I use documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dieckmann, may I also remind you that whenever there's any need to go into private session in order to make the pseudonym effective, that you immediately address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Witness 2, good morning again. We finished yesterday talking about an interview you have given to Bajrush Morina in the year of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness again this article; and, therefore, I would like to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you aware that Bajrush Morina published several critical articles about the party of Haradinaj in Bota Sot? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have access to those writings; however, I know that he continuously described events and made efforts to objectively present the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, you know Mr. Bajrush Morina as a friendly person, a person of good character?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to go to the first interview you have given to the ICTY in August 2007. In this interview - the Prosecution has already asked these questions, but I would like to repeat it again - in this interview, you had the opportunity to provide all information and facts you were aware and you knew at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you were aware that with this signature, you declared that this statement are the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Due to this statement, you have been contacted on or about the 1st of July, 2007, by telephone by a friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness -- the statements of the witness are in the first Prosecution binder. They're also available in the Albanian language. Perhaps the witness could have that made available to him in case he wants to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This would be excellent, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could then the first binder -- oh, it's already with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this would be at tab 3 of the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So, Witness 2, you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My last question was that I asked you that there have been a telephone call by a friend on or about the 1st of July, 2007. This -- the brother of this friend was working for the Bota Sot, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This friend who called you informed you that Bajrush Morina asked for your mobile number; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the friend asked you if you had any objection to giving it to him; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you replied that you did not have any objection to give the telephone number to Bajrush Morina; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. I asked him what was that about. He said: "I don't know. He just wants your number." And I said to him, "You can give it to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You remembered immediately who Bajrush Morina was when you received this call?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you were interested, you were curious what he really wants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he wanted my telephone number and wanted to speak with me, I was positive and I wanted to know what was that all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You don't know if that friend told Bajrush Morina you were travelling to The Hague, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The friend didn't know anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. But it is true that during these days, you were preparing for a trip to The Hague for a proofing session; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina called you back on 2nd of July, 2007; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And he used the number you authorised in the call with your mutual friend to use; true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, your question suggests calling back that the witness called him first. Can we clarify whether that's the case or did you misspeak?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've misspoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the question was about, Witness, whether Bajrush Morina called you on the 2nd of July, not in return to any call from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no call from my side; it was Bajrush who called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina explained to you that he could not talk on the phone more in detail, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And he wanted to meet you the very next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me that Minister Haraqija wanted to have a coffee with me the following day because he had something important to discuss with me. That's why he wanted a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, in the beginning, I thought you would need an introduction for a question which is the type of question we would expect in cross-examination; however, until now, you go through the statement which is in evidence. So if you'd like to cross-examine the witness, please refrain from repeating the whole of the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So your first reaction to this telephone -- to this telephone call was not just to hang up or to interrupt the call. My question is: Your reaction to this telephone call was not to hang up and stop the conversation when you heard what he was want from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My intention was not to hang up. We did talk and I explained that it was impossible to meet the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you did not immediately say that you did not wish to speak with anybody from Kosovo; you just said that you could not speak with him in the next day. True?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, I invited you not to go through the statement. Now you asked him whether he reacted by not having a conversation. That's so obvious from the evidence we have now. So if there's any reason to challenge that, please do so; but what we hear is just a repetition and some, I would say, some notorious facts. Of course, if you have a telephone conversation - and that's the evidence - then you have not refused to have the telephone conversation. That is clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would like to pose some questions just to see how the witness react in confrontation with this call. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What he did is he entered into a conversation with the person who called him. That's in evidence, that's clear. If you want to establish that, there's no need to do that because that is in evidence. If there's any challenge to what the witness said, please come to your point and focus on the issue you want to challenge. Please proceed. There's no need to emphasize matters in cross-examination. The evidence is as it is, and that is that the witness engaged in a conversation and did not stop, and that he did not say, "I never want to see you," but that he said "not tomorrow." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree with me that in this ICTY statement from August 2007, you did not state that Bajrush Morina asked you during this telephone call the question, "When are you going to The Hague"; true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, what is in the statement, the Chamber can read it. It's here. All the members of this Chamber are well-trained readers of statements. So, unless there's any reason, any ambiguity in it -- but please let's use our time in court in an efficient way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Then I will leave this statement from August 2007, and I would like to show the witness in private session, with your leave, the notice, Defence Exhibit number 4. This is notice of a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Karim Khan, and I am representing Mr. Haraqija. First of all, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I have only four questions for you, so I'll be very short and then you can go home. It's true to say that you have never met Mr. Haraqija; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's true to say that you've never spoken to Mr. Haraqija; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never spoken to him ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He has never threatened you in any way; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I never spoke to him, I don't know how he could have threatened me in any way; in other words, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, Witness, you'll be glad to see there's only three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So I have no more questions at all, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Saxon, the Bench has at this moment no questions. Do you have any need to put further questions to Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. We are in open session, you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 2. My colleague Mr. Khan --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You told my colleague Mr. Khan that you've actually never spoken with Mr. Haraqija. Do you recall saying that a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But in July of last year, did you receive through Mr. Morina -- I will rephrase my question. When, if ever, have you received a message from Mr. Haraqija?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a small point, but perhaps it can be added "if ever."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe that I added that in my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look in the transcript, it says "when, if ever ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said clearly earlier that I never contacted Mr. Haraqija and I was never contacted by him, but the messages came through Bajrush. Now, whether he conveyed the opinion and messages of Mr. Haraqija, that is clear, but I didn't have direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, wasn't the matter not already perfectly clear from the evidence in chief and the cross-examination, that although Witness 2 never spoke to Mr. Haraqija, that he gave his statement about messages and how he received them, et cetera. Is there any need to repeat, because Mr. Khan will ask again whether he ever spoke to him, and then it is like ping-pong rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate your point and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness Number 2, you mentioned a few moments ago that after investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor spoke with Mr. Morina, you had a conversation with Mr. Morina and Mr. Morina expressed to you that he feared for his security. My question, then, for you is: Who was Mr. Morina afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state clearly of whom he was afraid. His health was in very bad condition. He feared for his health. This is how I understood it, but I cannot state clearly of whom he was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my last question or my last few questions concerns --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I will ask to move into private session very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 2, when Bajrush Morina tells you something, do you believe in the truth of what he tells you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, how does this arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can explain that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a rather general question. Mr. Saxon, if I would ask you whether you believe me when I tell you something, what would be your answer, it depends on circumstances and what I tell you, isn't it? It's kind of a question of such a general nature that I have difficulties in understanding how it could assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then, if it won't assist the Chamber, I will withdraw my question, Your Honour, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps all this kerfuffle at the back is to clarify a particular point. It could be done by translation services at the end. But with your leave, perhaps I can just seek to clarify it. It arises out of page 22, line 8, of the transcript; and if I can read what the translation says, this is the witness speaking: "I said clearly earlier that I never contacted Mr. Haraqija and I was never contacted by him, but the messages came through Bajrush. Now, whether he conveyed the opinion and messages of Mr. Haraqija, that is clear; but I didn't have direct contact with him." Your Honour, the clarification is whether or not the witness said "that is clear," or whether, in fact, did he say "that is unclear."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness. Perhaps that is the easiest way of resolving the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 2, when you said now whether he conveyed the opinion and messages of Mr. Haraqija, then you added a few words. Could you repeat those words to the extent you still remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that part of the transcript, but I will try to say it again. As I said earlier, I didn't have direct contact with Haraqija; however, if the messages came through Bajrush, it was Bajrush who conveyed those messages, when he was present at the meeting in the country where I reside, then it is very clear that he conveyed those messages through Bajrush but not directly to me through telephone or direct conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This clarifies the matter, I take it, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 2, this concludes your testimony in this courtroom. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. I think all the curtains are down, so it would not in any way violate the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the ICTY for allowing me to participate in this session. I hope that justice will prevail and those who are not guilty will be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Mitford-Burgess, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that would be Ms. Angjelina Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have, then, that Mr. Mitford-Burgess will come at a later --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm also prepared to read the summaries of Witness 2's 92 ter statements into the record at a time that is convenient to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's perhaps if the -- is Mr. Usher aware that he should bring the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, to use our time as efficiently as possible, you read the summary of Witness 17, awaiting the arrival of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would now like to read a brief summary of what is now Exhibit P7, which is the ICTY witness statement of Witness 2 from the 14th of August, 2007. In summary, Your Honour, on the 2nd of July, 2007, Mr. Morina called Witness 2, and Mr. Morina told Witness 2: "I cannot talk with you on the phone. The minister of culture, Astrit Haraqija, wants to come and see you tomorrow." Mr. Morina told Witness 2 that the matter was urgent and that he wanted to talk with Witness 2 in the name of the Rugova family, knowing that Witness 2 was a strong supporter and follower of the former president, Ibrahim Rugova. Witness 2 told Mr. Morina that he would meet him on the 10th of July. Mr. Morina agreed, and over the next several days sent Witness 2 text messages to confirm that he, Mr. Morina, and the Minister Haraqija would be coming on the 10th. Witness 2 informed the authorities in the country where he resides about the telephone call from Mr. Morina. The authorities were concerned about Witness 2's security. Eventually, it was agreed that the meeting would take place under strictly controlled conditions and that the conversation would be recorded. Witness 2 met Mr. Morina on the 10th of July and the 11th of July, 2007. Both conversations were recorded. With your leave, Your Honours, I will now read a summary of Exhibit P8, which is the ICTY statement of Witness 2 provided on the 20th of September, 2007. This witness statement describes many of the same events described in Witness 2's earlier statement, Exhibit P7, but Exhibit P8 provides greater detail. In the second telephone call which Witness 2 received from Mr. Morina, Mr. Morina asked the witness when the witness was going to The Hague. At that moment, it became clear to Witness 2 that Mr. Morina and his associates knew that Witness 2 would be a witness in the Haradinaj trial. That upset Witness 2 very much and it also upset his wife. Witness 2 and Mr. Morina eventually agreed that Mr. Morina would arrive in the witness's country of residence on 10 July. Minister Haraqija would arrive on 11 July and they would depart on 12 July. Mr. Morina asked Witness Number 2 to reserve two hotel rooms of a good hotel, since the minister was of a certain rank and deserved a certain level of luxury. During the first meeting between Witness 2 and Morina on 10 July, Witness 2 understood that Mr. Morina had come to see the witness and pass on a message from Mr. Haraqija and a high-ranking official in UNMIK that there were three persons, including Witness 2, who could save Ramush Haradinaj by not testifying. Minister Haraqija had directed Mr. Morina to visit Witness 2 and pass this message to him. The goal of the message was to convince Witness 2 to withdraw his evidence from the trial of Ramush Haradinaj. Witness 2 told Mr. Morina that if he testified, he would not change his evidence and he could not be bought. Witness 2 met with Mr. Morina for a second time on 11 July. Minister Haraqija had not arrived. Mr. Morina had informed the minister that Witness 2 would not reconsider his decision to testify; and, therefore, Witness 2 assumed that the minister saw no point in speaking with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that. Perhaps I could have guidance, so that when it's my turn, do you want whole statements to be read out, or are summaries sufficient, just to guide my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, Mr. Saxon may not be so familiar and so acquainted with the practice in the trials I'm presiding over, that the summary could have been shorter. I mean, I think the core of the information could have been in 15 to 20 lines at most, but I didn't want to interrupt you. And short summaries, just sufficient for the public to understand what the testimony is about, rather than details as whether there were -- for example, the two hotel rooms and the quality of the hotel rooms are details that are not necessary. Apart from that, of course, they were elicited in chief which the public could hear. Are you ready to call your next witness, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, perhaps we could already first have the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Krasniqi. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Saxon, who is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, you need to speak a little bit louder so that the interpreters can hear you in the microphone. You might want to sit a little bit closer to the microphone. You can move your chair closer if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed, this witness will be providing evidence under Rule 92 ter. Would the Chamber prefer that I provide a short summary of each statement as we move along or should I wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the public to understand the testimony, it is preferred to have a short summary, not necessarily split up statement by statement, but just in a couple of lines to explain what we find in the 92 ter statement. Of course, a 92 ter statement which - let me just have a look - would be on your exhibit list as --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 18, 19, and 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 18, 19, and 20. All are already admitted into evidence. I think the interviews are 18 and 19; 20 is in the exhibit next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands, but the suggestion I would make is, as a matter of good practice, what I would respectfully submit is that summaries perhaps should be read before the witness enters or after the witness leaves. The reason for that is it seems to be a little unfair that the Prosecution perhaps can cherry-pick parts and summarize them. You've got the full statements before Your Honours. No objections at all for the summary, of course, but perhaps it could be done, if you're so minded, once the witness has left the courtroom after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in order for the public to understand what the testimony is about, to tell them at the end what they should have learned at the beginning in order to appreciate what the witness is telling is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's true. Your Honour's point is exceptionally valid; but that's why my principal submission, and I should have raised it earlier, is that summaries should be read in the absence of a witness because it does -- whether the Prosecution are doing it or the Defence are doing it, because otherwise it gives rise to the view that cherry-picking can take place that may affect the results in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I expect, as a matter of fact, the party summarizing the evidence to do that in a balanced way so that the public is informed. And if there's any complaint about that at any stage, I would invite the parties to disclose to the other party the summary so that comments could be made, Would you please include this, or leave that out, or to be too much of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, please read a short summary; and the summary, of course, is not evidence, Mr. Khan, that may be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will speak with a broad brush, Your Honour. Very briefly, this witness provided statements, two witness interviews, and a written witness statement to investigators of this office. The first one on the 7th of November, 2007. And by the way, Your Honours, I misspoke before. These are 65 ter numbers 17, 18, and 19. The second interview was on the 27th of May, 2008; and on the same day, an ICTY statement was provided. And in very broad terms, the witness describes how travel arrangements and authorisations are made or were made within the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sport when the witness worked there. The witness also describes -- and that would have been 65 ter 18, Your Honour. In 65 ter number 19, which is the ICTY witness statement of the 27th of May, the witness identifies two telephone numbers, one being hers at the Ministry of Culture and the second telephone number is that of Mr. Morina. And 65 ter 17 is an interview given by the witness on the 27th of May, 2008, in which the witness discusses a recorded intercept of a telephone call between herself and Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If I could ask the assistance of the usher, please, if the second -- actually, no, the first Prosecution binder could be provided to the witness; and if we could turn, please, if the usher could assist the witness, if we could turn to what is tab 18, the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, do you recall that two days ago, on Sunday, in my office here in the Tribunal in my presence and the presence of an interpreter and an investigator, you reviewed a statement that you -- an interview that you gave on the 7th of November, 2007? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could turn, please, to page 4 of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for those following along in English, this would be page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have page 4 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Saxon, that you want this not to be shown to the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention, Ms. Krasniqi, to line 27 of page 4, and this is line 26 of page 3. And I'm going to read to you several lines that go on to the next page, which would be page 5 in your version and page 4 in the English version. Starting at line 26 in the English version, the investigator asks: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The question was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This document is a written witness statement of Ms. Krasniqi provided on the 27th of May, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, do you recall reviewing this statement in my office on Sunday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does this statement accurately reflect your declaration?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does this statement accurately reflect what you would say if you were questioned or examined orally?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask that this statement be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P11, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document was already admitted. Now the attestation Rule 92 ter has been given; therefore, P11 is finally admitted under seal. Mr. Saxon, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions. Ms. Krasniqi, you just arrived, but we'll have a break first. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who will be the first to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Dieckmann. Ms. Krasniqi, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Dieckmann, who's counsel for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Krasniqi. My name is Jens Dieckmann. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Bajrush Morina, and I have just a few number of questions to you. If you do not understand a question, just indicate and I could repeat my question. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So, Madam, you have been deputy minister of culture in Kosovo; it's true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: From which period of time, in which period of time, you have been in this position?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You're not a member of the LDK, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could you explain to us which party you are belonging to at this time as a minister?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was a representative of the Demo-Christian Albanian party in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And Bajrush Morina worked for you as a political advisor; true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But he's not a member of your party at this time?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: He worked for you since spring-time 2005; is it true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You know him already before he started working for you; true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could it be that you know him since 2003/2004 election campaign?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You know him as a political journalist for the Bota Sot; true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Did you read frequently his articles in this newspaper during this time when you have been minister and before?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina has always been a supporter of the former President Rugova and his party; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina was never a member or in public a supporter of Ramush Haradinaj and his party, true, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And as a journalist, he has frequently written critical articles also against Ramush Haradinaj and his party; true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, you know the family of Bajrush Morina?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: He's married?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And he has -- he's the father of four children?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you know that he is also take care for his old and sick parents; true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, he does not have any criminal record in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You know Bajrush Morina as a friendly man, a person of good character; is it true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Krasniqi. I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But perhaps first we can go into private session for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Krasniqi, you'll also be glad to know that, hopefully, I won't take more than ten minutes or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Let me start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Astrit Haraqija never mentioned to you that he planned to travel to a third country; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct. He never mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Astrit Haraqija never mentioned to you that he knew Bajrush Morina was going to go to a third country; is that correct also?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct. He never mentioned that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You never saw a travel request signed by Astrit Haraqija seeking himself to go to that third country; is that also the truth?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And, similarly, it's true, is it not, that you never saw any travel request or note signed by Astrit Haraqija authorising Bajrush Morina to travel to that third country? That's also the truth, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's also truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Bajrush Morina told you that he had the permission of the minister to travel to that third country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But at no time did you verify that such permission had been given from any other source; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: All travel approvals, all travel requests that are processed must eventually be signed by Mr. Mon Zhubi, the permanent secretary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And no authorisation is valid until such signature is appended to a travel request; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, you explained that Mr. Morina is married, father of four children, and that he takes care of his sick parents as well. Back in July of last year, approximately how much did Mr. Morina earn a month as an advisor to you at the Ministry of Culture?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure, perhaps something around 400 Euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague asked you if Mr. Morina was always a supporter of the late-President Rugova and his party, and you answered yes. My question for you is: Even today, is President Rugova still revered in general by his supporters in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, this is more than true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In response to a question of my colleague Mr. Khan, you agreed that Mr. Morina had told you that before he travelled to the third country in July of last year, that Mr. Morina had the permission of the minister to travel. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When, if ever, did Mr. Morina tell you that he had been directed by the minister to travel to the third country?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just make sure that this is re-examination and, of course, it's not a licence for leading questions, and a question is not rendered non-leading simply by the addition "if ever." So I would ask that my friend exercise care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is there any basis at this moment already in the evidence of the witness for leading the witness in this respect? I invite you to explain where we find it; otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you will give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You see, Your Honour, my real principal and my principal objection is that when a party seeks to rely on 92 ter, the statements and the transcripts that have been properly attested and approved stand as examination-in-chief. It's not permissible for the Prosecution to have its cake and eat it. That is part of the testimony that's before Your Honours. If new matters arise out of cross-examination, of course, clarification can be sought; but it's also repeated on numerous occasions at page 2, page 8, page 13 of the 7th of November statement that this witness is saying that permission was granted. But, Your Honour, I don't see that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, your objection was about leading in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it now looks as if you add to that that the matter did not arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, there's two matters, in fact. It's leading which is the principal objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first one, I asked Mr. Saxon to find the place where is the basis, so as to make the question a follow-up question rather than a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The basis, Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The basis, Your Honour, can be found in what is now Exhibit P10, page 10 in the English version, lines 14 to 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P10 is the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From 27 May 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of 27 May, yes. We find that under tab 17, yes. It's not very clear to me. Could you please rephrase your question, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mention, Ms. Krasniqi, that the minister did not authorise Mr. Morina -- did not authorise the travel of Mr. Morina to go to the third country. Perhaps if I can put it more precisely, that -- that the minister, Mr. Haraqija, did not issue travel authorisation for Mr. Morina to go to a third country. However, can you tell us, please, whether, if in any way, to your knowledge, Mr. Haraqija was involved in Mr. Morina's trip to the third country?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not in my presence, so I couldn't know. I just know from talking with Bajrush that he was authorised by the minister, but not in my personal presence. I wasn't there as a witness to it, so I couldn't -- I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question for you, Ms. Krasniqi. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. When, if you do know, did President Rugova die?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to take you to part of what we find under tab 11 of the binder. Could the usher please assist the witness. Not to be shown to the public. Do you see the original and the handwriting at the bottom of this document? Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you say that Mr. Morina would travel to see a friend and that it was explained to you that it was for private reasons. Did anything come into your mind when you saw this document, where apparently a private visit to a friend is put in the context of travelling together with the minister, which at least could be considered to be something different from a private visit to a friend? Did anything come into your mind when you saw this as far as the reasons for the travel are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your testimony is that someone tells you that he'll privately see a friend in a third country; and that, although against the rules, permission is given for this travel to be funded, at least that's what's told to you; and then you see this document wherein apparently the minister accompanies the person on this private visit. And this did not raise any further thoughts with you as to the character of this visit?

utterances.speaker: ANGJELINA KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the -- have the questions put to the witness by the Bench raised any further need to put questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, in that case. Further cross-examination by Mr. Khan:

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Krasniqi, that document is not approved by the permanent secretary, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether it's this document on which we find handwriting of Mrs. Krasniqi; I'm asking when she saw that document whether that raised any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No questions. Yes, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No further questions for Mr. Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Krasniqi, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you for coming to the Hague and to testify; that is, to answer both questions of the parties and the Bench. I would like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is excused and may be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. At this time, the Prosecution would call Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could use the time that you read a short summary of the witness so that the public is informed, and even the wish of Mr. Khan it not to be read in the presence of the witness would be met. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The statement of Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess describes how he and another colleague in the Office of the Prosecutor obtained several items of evidence that are relevant to this case, both statements from witnesses as well as documentary evidence. And in his statement, Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess produces this material for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. May the next witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mitford-Burgess. Before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitford-Burgess. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Saxon, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mitford-Burgess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps, again, with the usher's assistance, if the first binder could be placed in front of Mr. Mitford-Burgess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before we begin, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, I would simply ask you to remember to take care not to reveal any identifying details of the protected witness or the protected witness's residence. If you can turn, please, to what is tab 5 in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Prosecution 65 ter number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, this is a declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if this could not be published to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a declaration signed by you on the 16th of July, 2008. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my question for you is: Will you attest that this written statement accurately reflects your declaration?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And will you attest that this written statement accurately reflects what you would say if you were questioned or examined verbally today?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would ask that this exhibit be given an exhibit number as well as the associated exhibits, which, if you'd like, I can read the 65 ter numbers of those exhibits into the record, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The exhibits associated with this -- with the statement of Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess are 65 ter numbers 1, 2, 7 through 11, 13 through 16, 20 through 23, and 26 through 28. Pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision of 2 September 2008, these exhibits would be admitted pursuant -- along with the written statement of Mr. Peter Mitford-Burgess. Your ruling had been deferred on Exhibit -- 65 ter Exhibits 1 through 2 and 29 through 30, but it's the Prosecution understanding that given the Trial Chamber's decision of last week not to exclude exhibits -- 65 ter Exhibits 1 and 2, then it would be appropriate to admit them at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Defence whether there are any objections, objections which are not yet dealt with by motions to exclude evidence, but for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No objections for the Defence for Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so I don't create confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- my colleague, Mr. Smith, has reminded me that 65 ter Exhibits number 29 and 30 were admitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As numbers P2 and P3, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Then, when you referred to Exhibits 1 and 2, you included 1A, B, C, and 2A, B, C, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, I don't know whether the 1A, B, C need separate exhibit numbers or whether they can be taken together; that is, transcript, audio-recording, and video-recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, for 65 ter 1A, B, C uploaded together, Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit Number P12, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P12 is admitted under seal. 2A, B, C would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P13, Your Honours, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P13 is admitted into evidence under seal. Now 65 ter number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For all the associated exhibits, Mr. Registrar will prepare a list assigning provisionally exhibit numbers, and then we'll deal with them once we have that on paper. I already draw the attention of you, Mr. Registrar, to the order in which not 7 but 8 to 11, 13, and 15 are admitted under seal; and for 21, 22, and 23, it's also ordered that they would be admitted under seal. We'll receive a list from Mr. Registrar and then we'll formally decide on admission; but in the absence of any objections, the decision to be expected is once numbers have been assigned, that they'll all be admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek the Chamber's guidance very briefly on a point of procedure. There are two exhibits on the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list, which I could hypothetically tender through this witness. One of them is Exhibit -- 65 ter Exhibit 31, which is a confidential list that was filed in the case of Prosecutor versus Haradinaj. The second exhibit would be 65 ter Exhibit 32, which was another filing in the case of Mr. Haradinaj. It's a decision on the Prosecution's application for protective measures. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- my first suggestion was that perhaps the Chamber could simply take judicial notice of these -- of these court documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, can I say as well, as a form of concession, that, of course, the Witness 2 was a protected witness and was subject to the relevant orders as contended by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dieckmann, do you take the same position?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, then, it appears to be an agreed fact that Witness 2 was a witness in the Haradinaj case and that his protection, including not to reveal his identity, was ordered by the Trial Chamber. That is now an agreed fact. Then I think that there's no need to further tender through the bar table the documents appearing under numbers 31 and 32. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the Chamber's leave, then, for several minutes to tender -- to attempt to tender two more exhibits through Mr. Mitford-Burgess?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, if you could turn please to tab 11 in that binder in front of you. And, Mr. Mitford-Burgess, these are a series of travel-related documents obtained from the Ministry of Culture in Kosovo. If you turn to what I believe is the 12th page in your version which has --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if this please not be published to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see an ERN number 06244292 in the upper right-hand corner. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we please move -- I'm sorry, is the Chamber with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see Judge Moloto is now with me. It should be about the 12th page into this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I look to my left and I'm familiar with the document anyhow, so I'll find it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May we please move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, did you receive the permission from the police from this third country to use this material in further investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I don't think it was a case of the authorities there giving us explicit permission. I believe that in the receipt of the material, it was envisaged that we would use it in any investigation we undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The use of this document, it was your own decision during this interview to use this?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: During the course of the interview, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you didn't get any order to use it from superiors?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the fact you have received information, could you briefly illustrate what kind of information you received about the legal nature of this material?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: We received information from a police officer from that country, who was responsible for the obtaining of this material, and that it was obtained in accord with the laws of that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you have not been aware that, in fact, in this country, there is no parliament law to govern the production of this kind of recordings --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, if we first allow Mr. Dieckmann to finish his question, and then I'd like to hear your objection. Was that the whole of your question, Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: These kind of recordings in the conduct of police activities, police investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My objection is that within the question of my learned colleague is a legal conclusion that I don't believe has been established yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, Mr. Dieckmann is asking for an awareness of the non-existence of a particular law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That appears to be, yes, the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that seems to be a factual question whether a law exists or not, whether that law would apply. Whether the non-existence of such a law would have an impact on the legal or illegal character of what was undertaken is, of course, a different matter and requires legal expertise. But awareness of the existence of a law governing certain matter is a question of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, during the conduct of this interview, you have been aware that Bajrush Morina was talking about an interview he made with the Witness 2 in 2002 before you confronted him with the material you received from the third country? Could you remember this?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, I will not insist, but at least the effect of the objection by Mr. Saxon is that your question has not been answered. If that is what you wish, fine; if that's not what you -- perhaps that's what Mr. Saxon wished to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Awareness of the existence of a law was your question, Mr. Saxon opposed, the objection was denied, and then you moved on to a next question, which is fine with me --

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the laws of this country. All I can say is and reiterate that I was told by a police officer from that country that their activities were in accord with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, would you be so cautious when referring to the country at page 64, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, being informed that such an interview should have taken place, did you conduct any further investigations after this interview from the 26th of October, 2007, with regard to this interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, in fact, you completely ignored this interview in your further investigations?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I had no reason to dispute the fact that such an interview had taken place between Mr. Morina and Witness 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, could I invite you to read again page 65, line 1 and following, that question. Apparently, the witness understood your question; I did not. But it may be that it has not been transcribed accurately, I do not know; but could you perhaps rephrase the question so that not only the witness but I also understand the question, and then seek confirmation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, my question on page 65, line 1 and 2 should be: Being informed by Bajrush Morina that such an interview should have taken place, did you start any kind of further investigations with relation to this interview in your further investigation after the 26th of October, 2007?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: In respect of confirming whether or not such an interview took place between Mr. Morina and Witness 2 in 2002, I did not. We accepted on face value from what he said that such an interview took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I understand you. You did not further investigate whether that interview took place or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have been misled by the word "interview" because "interview" have several meanings in this context, journalistic and investigative. Mr. Khan, do you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: With your leave, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, Mr. Khan is counsel for Mr. Haraqija and he'll now cross-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I start the cross-examination, with Your Honour's leave, perhaps I could go into -- we could go into private session for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The ruling just given, of course, does not mean that to the extent not necessary we could not respect the privacy of the person involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm being rather dense, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ruling is clear that there are no limits, but my invitation is to not unnecessarily add to what might be not sought by Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, my name is Karim Khan and I'm counsel for Astrit Haraqija. I have some questions for you. It's correct, isn't it, that you are a very experienced police officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And prior to coming to the Yugoslav Tribunal in 2000, you were a police officer in your native New Zealand; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: How many years have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Twenty-nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you were the officer in charge, the investigative officer in charge, in this contempt case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You had overall supervision for ensuring that proper investigative practices were implemented to ensure the integrity of the proceedings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And also knowing that there was a duty to obtain the best evidence for Their Honours to make an informed decision; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: On the 19th of December, 2007, you interviewed Steven Schook; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Schook held a high office in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, he was the second-most senior United Nations official; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He was appointed directly by the special representative -- appointed directly by the Secretary-General of the United Nations; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you suspected that he was perhaps involved in contempt under Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the basis of that was the hearsay evidence of the second accused in this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And based upon that evidence, you required him to attend for questioning, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can show the officer an interview and get him to verify that it's a true record of what transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the assistance of the usher, there are copies for the Chamber. It's in the Prosecution's -- no, it's not. And one for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, just glancing at that document is it correct to say that that is a true and full transcript of the interview that you yourself conducted with Steven Schook in December of last year?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You can look at page 5 if you wish, but it's correct, isn't it, that the deputy SRSG stated, unequivocally, that he never had any conversation with anybody in respect of any witness in the Haradinaj case. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You may wish to glance at page 10, but you will no doubt recollect that he was emphatic when he said that he never instructed anybody to seek an employee to speak with any protected witness relevant to this case. You can see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that's what he said?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And by that, of course, you know that he was denying that he ever told Astrit Haraqija to speak with the -- sorry. Let me put that again. By that, you know that he was denying that he ever told my client, Mr. Haraqija, to tell Bajrush Morina to speak with the protected witness in this case? You know that was his answer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He was emphatic that he had never told anybody at all that the protected witness in this case should not come and give evidence? He never tried -- he never conveyed a message to anybody that the protected witness in this case should be persuaded not to give evidence. That was his clear and unequivocal case, was it not? That was his evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender that transcript of interview as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: There's no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- name of Mr. Schook is on the witness list as well as a 92 bis witness. Now, does it make sense -- I mean, now it's his statement on paper without the attestations. Would it not be a better idea to have it admitted under Rule 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then, of course, what we do know is that at least now Mr. Mitford-Burgess said that this is the statement. Could the parties agree that what has been shown to the witness at this moment is exactly the same statement as the Defence tenders under 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would have been, of course, most logical had we complied or been able to comply with the requirements of 92 bis. Unfortunately, we haven't been able to contact and find the address of the witness. We sought it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say he's off the list --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He's off the list for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, it makes sense. Mr. Saxon, any objection against the admission of the statement as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, because it was the Trial Chamber's decision that the statement of Mr. Schook could be admitted if it was certified under Rule 92 bis, and we have not received such a certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it true that the Defence has sought to introduce the statement through Rule 92 bis, that they have failed to comply with the requirements under Rule 92 bis, and that now - and that's, of course, the issue, Mr. Khan - that you now seek to introduce this same statement through the witness, Mr. Mitford-Burgess?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am rather surprised. No doubt, it was my confusion. But my very clear recollection was that my learned friend was not objecting to the interview of Steven Schook, but he was objecting to the second interview that I recalled. But, Your Honour, be that as it may, there are a number of points I could make. The witness who took this interview is available for cross-examination; he's the man in the dock. This document doesn't just have external indicia of reliability. It has intrinsic indicia of reliability because it's an interview, it was tape recorded; and, most importantly, it was not taken by the party using it, it was taken by the adversary party. So, in my submission, it's very clear that this by any standard must be admissible. Perhaps one could step back for a moment and wonder under what basis does the Prosecution seek to exhibit the interviews of my client. They're not taken under Rule 92 bis. They're taken because there is a witness who conducted those interviews that presents them as evidence in court. In my submission, the same logic would pertain to the admission in court now as an exhibit from the witness, from the investigator, who conducted that interview. For the life me, I don't see how those issues can be logically separated. There are intrinsic issues of reliability, and, as I said, Your Honour, it's taken by the Prosecution, not by the Defence. There are no -- there are a number of different ways to seek admission under the Rules of this Tribunal. 89(C) is there of course. There are other modalities. But this is not a statement, this is an interview, which is verifiable, which was taken by the Prosecution, and which was in their possession. So, in my submission it's probative, it's relevant, and it's clearly admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would not immediately decide on the admission. We'd like to further consideration the situation where several rules seem to be in play. The Chamber would like to take its time to consider whether this is admissible evidence, yes or no. Therefore, for the time being, Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number so that the statement is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number D1, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, D1 is now marked for identification. You briefly raised the matter of admissibility. Mr. Khan said quite a lot about it. Mr. Dieckmann has not expressed himself yet on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would join the submissions of my learned friend Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
