utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Saxon, do you feel any need to offer further submissions on the issues raised by Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I've expressed myself clearly that the wholesale admission of this statement would be contrary to the order of this Chamber, and that is because Rule 92 bis prescribes specific criteria for admission; and in this case, the gentleman is not available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At the same time, Mr. Khan has explained why under the present circumstances, even by not applying Rule 92 bis, that nevertheless this document, not under Rule 92 bis but as a document introduced through this witness, should be admitted. And I just wondered whether you wanted to further respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would respond this way. Suppose the situation were reversed and the Prosecution sought permission to tender the suspect interview of a witness with a great deal of inculpatory information against an accused and that witness was not appearing here in this court, the statement was not certified in any way under 92 bis, in my respectful submission, that request by the Prosecution would be summarily denied. So I believe we're in a similar situation here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to belabour the point as -- or engage in ping-pong, as Your Honour put it quite properly. But two points that Your Honour had asked be carefully considered when deciding this matter. The Rules under Rule 42 and 43 were complied with. The Martic case makes it very clear that there's no absolute right to cross-examination, and I'm not going to go into all the details about that. In relation to the last point, my learned friend hasn't addressed how this is logically distinguishable from the Prosecution putting in suspect interviews either. But, Your Honour, I don't need to belabour the point. I'll be happy with what Your Honours decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will decide on the matter and we'll give a ruling on it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if you give me a moment just to try and organize myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we also ask you, Mr. Khan, how much time you would still need for planning purposes? We are close to the moment where we usually have a second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it will be about five or ten minutes. I'll try to be less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be five were ten minutes, this would be the last Prosecution witness, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, then, perhaps it's good to see whether you can finish in five to ten minutes and then have the break, and then after that hear the case presentation by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll try to be -- I'll try to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, it's correct, is it not, that no charges were brought against Steven Schook? He hasn't been indicted by this court, has he?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir, he has not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you accept that the evidence that gave rise to the suspect interview in relation to that gentleman was comprised of hearsay evidence from the second accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You conducted surveillance of his phone and there was no link of any impropriety between him and my client; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You conducted searchs of UNMIK offices, looked at the computer, and there was no evidence incriminating my client at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: On the 28th of October, 2007, it's correct, is it not, that you interviewed Mr. Veli Bytyqi? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You were present in that interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you spoke to him in relation to the investigation that you were conducting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: He states that he was present -- he told you that he was present in Peja during the opening of a theatre. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You are of the view that my client incited the second accused in this case during the opening of that theatre in Peja, that he incited him to commit a contempt of this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Our information was that there was a discussion at a cafe in Peja which a number of people were present, including Mr. Morina and Mr. Haraqija, when this subject of which you're talking about was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just be rather plain in case there be any doubt. You say that it was during that event in Peja that my client told the second accused that he should interfere with a witness protected by this Court. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: That's our belief, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I have problems. I'm not aware that Mr. Mitford-Burgess has any case to present here. So whether it's the case in what he says or whether he reports on what he learned during interviews is a matter to be clearly distinguished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, it's correct, is it not, that Veli Bytyqi says that he was present in Peja and there was no mention that he heard -- he didn't hear any mention of any protected witness. You remember him saying that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He said a number of things. Yes, I agree with you, he did say that he didn't hear it, but he also said that it's possible that the discussion could have taken place and he was not a party to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm not suggesting at all that Mr. Bytyqi is omniscient and can hear everything; but it was very clear from what he told you that he was sitting next to Mr. Haraqija during that event, he was close to Mr. Haraqija, and he didn't hear any mention of any protected witness. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: He didn't exactly say where he was sitting. He said he was with the group and he didn't hear such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And he didn't recall any mention of the ICTY or criminal proceedings here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I am right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness can be shown the interview of Veli Bytyqi. This is the interview that I understood the Prosecution was objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we first -- we know what the -- apart from the witness looking at it, could we first hear the objection which are, I take it, not related in any way to what this witness could tell us about it. Mr. Saxon, we do understand that you would have objections against admission of Mr. Bytyqi's interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yeah, I make the same objections, Your Honour, because the Trial Chamber in its decision of 5 September 2008 said that it would admit this interview of Mr. Veli Bytyqi into evidence if the witness would appear in court for cross-examination and any questioning by the Judges, and that witnesses will attest that the written statements or transcripts are accurate. Now, that has not happened and it appears that that is not going to happen with respect to this interview, this transcript of an interview, with Mr. Veli Bytyqi, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, at least there is a difference, I would say, with the previous matter, which is that the Chamber ruled that the statement of Mr. Bytyqi would be admissible under the condition that he would appear and be available for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the case. Your Honour, the difficulty is that I had information from Kosovo - I can't give evidence - but he viewed himself as being a Prosecution witness. And given the imminence of the trial, I couldn't get a letter from the Prosecution, I didn't even try to get a letter from the Prosecution, because by the time it came to my notice it was the weekend. But, Your Honours, the arguments in addition to the points raised earlier are that if one sees from the face of the document, this was annex K to the Prosecution's papers that they submitted to His Honour Judge Moloto to get the indictment confirmed. It seems completely inequitable, in my respectful submission, that the Prosecution, on the one hand, can use this evidence to haul my client here to The Hague and yet object for the same evidence being put forward by the Defence to exculpate their client. It seems to be a rather unfortunate position, and one, in my respectful submission, that is rather bereft in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the argument is, I would say, pretty straightforward. How could you rely on this evidence to get the indictment confirmed and now object against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I certainly cannot deny, Your Honour, the fact that the Prosecution has relied on this interview in the past, and I take my learned colleague's point that there is an inconsistency in the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the admission of this evidence together with the statement of Mr. Schook. At the same time, in view of the exchange of arguments, the Chamber does not at this moment prevent you from asking questions about the statement which will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. Before I forget, in relation to the first interview from the UNMIK official that is going to be decided upon, I would just emphasize that should you decide to grant the application to give it an exhibit number, it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good that you remind us. Mr. Registrar, the document that is I think D1, marked for identification, should remain under seal. Then perhaps it would be most practical to ask Mr. Registrar to assign an MFI number to this document as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number D2, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also under seal, Mr. Registrar. Then that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I'm again looking at the clock. If it would take more than five to six minutes, we'll need to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. I think we ought to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have the break and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, you earlier indicated that you would need five to ten minutes. Would you please stay within those limits. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, in this way, minutes are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are lost. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Why did it take you until August of 2007, Witness, to seek to get authorisation from a Trial Chamber in the ICTY to commence investigations in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I didn't come in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If my learned colleague is going to question the very legal foundation of the OTP's investigation in this case, which really means the very legal foundation of this entire matter, it seems to me that this would have been more appropriate for a separate motion, and I just don't know if that is the intent of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, would you please focus on facts in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has come up already in cross-examination, and I also notified my learned friend, back in July, about my position. Indeed, he was refusing to give me the date of the Trial Chamber's order to commence investigations unless he asked -- and he wanted to know the reason why. Let me put it more neutrally. And I was very candid with him that one of the reasons why I want the date is the legality of what has transpired. Now, this is the officer who was in charge of the investigation. I don't see it's a completely improper question. Your Honours, if you think it is, of course, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And once the Prosecution had my learned friend's reasons, the date was given to my learned friend immediately, and my learned friend would have had time to have addressed this matter if he had so chosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the objection is denied. Mr. Khan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you answer, why did it take so long between your suspicions being aroused and seeking authorisation from the ICTY Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I first became involved in this investigation on the 30th of August of 2007, when I received instructions. What happened factually and legally prior to that, I was not a party to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that my client's mobile telephone was monitored, it was under surveillance, in October 2007?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that from that surveillance, you obtained no evidence that was supporting -- capable of supporting the allegations that my client was involved in a contempt of this court?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know why an order for surveillance was not done -- was not sought in August or September of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You executed a search warrant on the department of which my client was the minister; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You were given cooperation during that search; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you check my client's computer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you check the fax machine for incoming and outgoing faxes?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you speak and interview the permanent secretary in charge of that ministry?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You are quite willing, it seems, to prefer an indictment against my client based on hearsay evidence; that's a fair assessment, isn't it, officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I presume that hearsay evidence is one of the ingredients of the material that went to the Court seeking an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you were happy to prefer that hearsay evidence as a basis to convict an innocent man, a man of previous good character; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Well, happiness is not an issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You felt professionally satisfied that you could in good faith submit a case based on hearsay evidence, despite the fact you didn't conduct a very thorough investigation. Would you agree with that or would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I agree and disagree. By all means, we used hearsay evidence, but I don't agree that it was an unthorough investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness can be shown tab 11. It's the document under seal, with the manuscript writing on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mitford-Burgess, did you find it? It is the first document under tab 11, first binder, and the handwriting Mr. Khan was referring to is found in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, where did you obtain this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I understand this was provided to us by the Witness Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know where she got that document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I presume it was part of the records in her office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Do you know whose writing is on the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I believe it is hers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The same day a second -- a search warrant was executed at the ministry offices in Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Various documents were seized; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: This document was not amongst them, was it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, you were told by the second accused in this case when you interviewed him, that the reason he went to the third country was because he wished to check the veracity of an article he had written back in 2002. Do you remember him saying that at the outset of the interview?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Have you ever read that article?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: In fact, it's fair to say that the Prosecution didn't even have possession of that document until it was given by the Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You were quite content with your theory of the case, that this meeting was all about witness intimidation and the involvement of Astrit Haraqija, and you didn't even seek to explore other possibilities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: The witness said, initially, that he had gone to the third country to discuss the article that he had written in 2002. Later in the interview, he conceded that that was not the case, that his real intention in going to the third country to see Witness 2 was a directive from his supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. Officer, that, of course, was after you confronted the second accused with the surveillance that was conducted in the third country; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Is it a rare occurrence in your professional experience, in New Zealand and in the Tribunal, for an accused who is -- for an individual that is confronted with an inconsistent account to run back and seek refuge in that previous different account?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Are you meaning that, from the outset, he gave us one story and then when we confronted him with the facts, he changed the story?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, the evidence, is it not, officer, is that he went back to an account that was consistent in broad terms to what was recorded? That's what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You didn't try and allow the second accused to develop his account before you confronted him with the surveillance evidence, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I still don't understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Let me try it again. It's my fault. Please do bear with me. You did not explore in interview or at any time the second accused's statement in interview that the primary reason he went to the third country was to do with journalism? Is that clear enough, officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes. And, yes, we did explore with him the reason he went to the third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And is it a rare occurrence in your professional experience that when an individual is confronted with a recording that is different from the account that they give, that sometimes they seek refuge in the previous recorded account, whether it's true or not? It happens, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I can only speak on this occasion about the facts of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, officer, I'm asking you in your professional experience as somebody well-versed and well experienced in investigating criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: My only answer is that the accused had the opportunity to give us an account of his activities; after doing so, we confronted him with a tape-recording of a conversation, after which he gave us another account of his activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, I'll move on. I don't want to belabour the point. I think Their Honours have got the point that I was trying to make. You knew that Mr. Morina was a journalist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You knew that he was in strait and financial circumstances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You knew that he wrote an article about the third country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you think he did that out of the goodness of his heart, or did you think it was part of his professional activity as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I can only presume it was part of his professional activity as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you, at any time in your investigations in this case, explore and investigate any other motive that the witness -- that the second accused could have had to go to the third country? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, if my learned friend could simply clarify who he is referring to by the second accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that he's referring to Mr. Morina because he would not refer to his own client as the second accused, and there are only two. That is how I understand your questions, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour is spot on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, you didn't investigate any other possibility in this case except that this was a contempt of court from start to finish. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And the reason for that is you were having hellish problems in the Haradinaj case, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in the Haradinaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that under Rule 77 of the Tribunal, the OTP is required to get permission from a Trial Chamber before they can initiate investigations into contempt? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: That's the last time, Your Honour. I'm tremendously sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what happens if you go beyond your five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's also what happens when I'm try to rush to finish in the five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Officer, were you seeking to use the investigative agencies of the third state to conduct investigation by proxy?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Saxon, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe I can do it in 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do it as quickly as could be reasonably expected from you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitford-Burgess, a few minutes ago my learned colleague Mr. Khan asked you about the interview that you carried out with Mr. Morina back in October of last year, and you described how, initially, Mr. Morina told you that he had gone to a third country - to the third country in this case - to have a meeting related to an article because he needed to discuss an article that he had published. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you explained that later, however, when Mr. Morina was confronted with some of the recording of one of those meetings, Mr. Morina explained that actually he had been directed by his supervisor to go to that third country for the meeting. That was your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you -- are you familiar with the contents of the recorded meetings in the third country?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, please, is there -- to your knowledge, is there anywhere in these -- any indication in these recordings of those two meetings that Mr. Morina's purpose in going to that third country and meeting with the protected witness was to discuss an article published back in 2002?

utterances.speaker: PETER MITFORD-BURGESS
utterances.text: No, not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. My colleague -- if you could turn to tab 11. I don't know if you still have that in front of you. And if you turn to the first page of tab 11, and my colleague asked you some questions about this document. It's document from the Ministry of Culture dated the 6th of July, 2007. And my colleague referred you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I have to object because I think this is -- the question was misleading regarding the content of the conversation on the 10th and 11th of July, 2007, because, in fact, in the revised transcripts, you find parts where my client was talking about the interview with the Witness Number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, reading the question, Mr. Saxon refers to tab 11, asked whether the witness still has it in front of him, directed him to the first page, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, the question before. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're, of course, supposed to object when the question has not been answered and not after the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, whether any indication is found in the recordings, of course, the Chamber can read as well. So whether there is any indication or if there would be any specific indication, we would have expected you to raise the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: -- you to page 92, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: "Now can you tell us, please, is there -- to your knowledge, is there anywhere any in these -- indication in these recordings of those two meetings that Mr. Morina's purpose in going to that third country and meeting with the protected witness was to discuss an article published in 2002?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you read, your speed of speech goes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And due to my information from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to give the reasons for the decision as I announced yesterday. The reasons for the denial of Astrit Haraqija's and Bajrush Morina's joint request for certification for appeal of Trial Chamber's decision on Bajrush Morina's request for a declaration of inadmissibility and exclusion of evidence dated the 28th of August, 2008, I refer to that as the motion for certification. The reasons are the following: On the 4th of September, 2008, the joint Defence submitted the motion for certification, requesting leave to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision on Bajrush Morina's request for a declaration of inadmissibility and exclusion of evidence, the impugned decision. In support, the Defence argues that: A, the Trial Chamber erred in failing to realize or failing to properly consider that the correct translation of the suspect interview with the accused Morina is an area of clear dispute between the parties; B, the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that the corrected, more prejudicial version was the correct version without its own independent verification thereof by appointing an independent translator to listen to the audio recording of the suspect interview and review written transcript for accuracy; C, the Trial Chamber applied an incorrect standard in respect of the required voluntariness of the waiver of the right to the assistance of counsel. According to the Defence, these issues would significantly affect the outcome of the trial as well as the fair conduct of the proceedings. It argues that the Trial Chamber's errors clearly constitute a ground of appeal post-judgement which can possibly be avoided if the issue is resolved now. Finally, the Defence also points out that since the trial is due to be held only during this week, an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. On September the 5th, 2008, the Prosecution filed its response opposing the motion for certification. The Prosecution submits that the Defence never disputed the accuracy of the revised translation prior to the issuance of the impugned decision, nor that it had sought verification of the translation by an independent interpreter. Moreover, the Prosecution argues that the Defence has not explained how the Trial Chamber misapplied the law applying "an incorrect standard." The Prosecution concludes that the Defence has not demonstrated that the fairness and expeditiousness of these proceedings would be served by certifying this appeal, which is the first prong of the requirements under Rule 73(B). The Chamber notes that a proper request for certification is "not concerned with whether a decision was correctly reasoned or not. That is a matter for appeal, be it an interlocutory appeal or one after final judgement has been rendered. Rule 73(B) concerns the fulfilment of two criteria, after which the Trial Chamber may decide to certify an interlocutory appeal." Accordingly, according to Rule 73(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, "decisions on all motions are without interlocutory appeal, save with certification by the Trial Chamber which may grant such certification if the decision involves an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial and for which, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings." The fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. The Chamber concurs with the Prosecution that a thorough reading of the Defence submissions made prior to the impugned decision reveals that the Defence did not submit that it took issue with the accuracy of the Prosecution's revised translation, in particular as regards the expression "maybe later," nor has the Defence on a prior occasion requested that the revised translation be verified by an independent interpreter. Footnote 2 of the Defence submission of the 4th of August, 2008, reads: "The Defence has as of yet been unable to verify whether this corrected version is, indeed, an accurate transcription and translation of the audio of the interview. If the translation is in dispute, it may need to be submitted to an independent interpreter for verification. Nonetheless, even assuming that the language in the latest English transcript is correct, the Defence submits that the ambiguity of the language of Mr. Morina's purported waiver remains unchanged." This is the end of the reading of footnote 2. Moreover, the Chamber finds that the Defence has not sufficiently substantiated its claim that the Chamber applied an incorrect standard in its impugned decision. Therefore, the Chamber is not satisfied that the Defence has demonstrated that the impugned decision suffers from such a flaw in its factual or legal reasoning that the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial has been called into question. I now move to materially advance the proceedings. Having found that the first of the two requirements under Rule 73(B) has not been met and considering that an application for certification must satisfy both requirements cumulatively, there would be no need for the Chamber to address the issue of whether immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber would materially advance the proceedings. Nevertheless, the Chamber finds that the Defence has also failed to satisfy this requirement. The certification motion was filed two working days prior to commencement of the case and about one week before its conclusion. It is, therefore, difficult to conceive how resolution by the Appeals Chamber could materially advance the proceedings. On the contrary, in the Chamber's view allowing an interlocutory appeal at this time would cause an unnecessary delay in concluding the proceedings in the present case. This concludes the reasons for the denial of the certification sought. We have five minutes left. I think it would not be very wise to invite the Defence to start --
